core_theory: The four fundamental operations on numbers: addition subtraction multiplication and division. Forms the numerical foundation for all mathematics.
The study of mathematical symbols and rules for manipulating those symbols. Enables generalisation from arithmetic to variables and equations.

description: Points and curves on the x-y plane
core_theory: A system that uses pairs of numbers called coordinates to uniquely determine the position of points in a plane. Bridges algebra and geometry.
In any right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a² + b² = c².
Two triangles are similar when their corresponding angles are equal. Their corresponding side lengths are proportional giving a constant ratio r/h.
The study of relationships between angles and side lengths of triangles. Defines the six trigonometric functions from ratios of sides in a right triangle.

description: Circle of radius 1 for angle definition
core_theory: A circle of radius 1 centred at the origin used to define trigonometric function values for any angle including those beyond 90 degrees.
A function f: A → B assigns to each element of domain A exactly one element of codomain B. Captured by notation f(x) where x is the input variable.
The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is the value L that f(x) gets arbitrarily close to as x gets arbitrarily close to a. Written lim(x→a) f(x) = L.
A function f is continuous at x = a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a). Informally: the function can be drawn without lifting the pencil.
The derivative f'(x) = lim(h→0)[f(x+h)-f(x)]/h measures the instantaneous rate of change of f at x. Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line.

description: Derivative of x raised to n
core_theory: The power rule states that d/dx[x^n] = n·x^(n-1) for any real number n. It is the most frequently applied differentiation rule.
The product rule states that the derivative of f·g is f'·g + f·g'. It applies whenever two differentiable functions are multiplied together.
The quotient rule states that d/dx[f/g] = (f'·g - f·g')/g². It applies whenever one differentiable function is divided by another.
The chain rule states that d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x). In Leibniz notation: dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx). Essential for any nested function.
A technique to find dy/dx when y is defined implicitly by an equation in x and y. Both sides are differentiated with respect to x and the chain rule applied to y terms.
Functions sin(x) cos(x) tan(x) sec(x) csc(x) cot(x) defined for all real x using the unit circle. Periodic with period 2π for sin and cos.
d/dx[sin(x)] = cos(x) and d/dx[cos(x)] = −sin(x). All other trig derivatives follow from these two using quotient and chain rules.
Functions of the form f(x) = a^x where a > 0 and a ≠ 1. The natural exponential f(x) = e^x is its own derivative: d/dx[e^x] = e^x.
The logarithm log_a(x) is the inverse of a^x. The natural logarithm ln(x) satisfies d/dx[ln(x)] = 1/x and is the inverse of e^x.

description: Finding unknown rates from known rates
core_theory: Problems where two or more quantities change over time and are related by an equation. Differentiate the equation implicitly with respect to t to find the unknown rate.
Finding the values of x that maximise or minimise a function f(x). Requires finding critical points where f'(x) = 0 and testing them with the second derivative.

description: Points where derivative is zero or undefined
core_theory: A point x = c is a critical point of f if f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) is undefined. Critical points are candidates for local maxima, minima, or saddle points.
If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0 then c is a local minimum. If f''(c) < 0 then c is a local maximum. If f''(c) = 0 the test is inconclusive.
Using limits derivatives and second derivatives to determine domain intercepts asymptotes intervals of increase/decrease concavity and inflection points of a function.
The integral ∫f(x)dx is the reverse of differentiation. The definite integral ∫[a,b]f(x)dx represents the signed area under f between x=a and x=b.
An indefinite integral ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x) and C is the constant of integration. Represents a family of antiderivatives.

description: Numerical value of integral over interval
core_theory: The definite integral ∫[a,b]f(x)dx is a number giving the signed area under f from a to b. Evaluated via the Fundamental Theorem: F(b) - F(a).
The substitution method: let u = g(x) so du = g'(x)dx transforming ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx into ∫f(u)du. The reverse of the chain rule for integration.
The rule ∫u·dv = u·v − ∫v·du derived from the product rule. Used for integrals of products of functions like x·e^x or x·sin(x).
The FTC has two parts: (1) d/dx[∫[a,x]f(t)dt] = f(x); (2) ∫[a,b]f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a). It unifies the two central operations of calculus.
The area between f(x) and g(x) from a to b is ∫[a,b]|f(x)-g(x)|dx. Requires finding intersection points and determining which function is on top.
Volumes of solids formed by rotating a curve about an axis. Computed by the disk/washer method or cylindrical shell method using definite integrals.

description: Ordered lists and their partial sums
core_theory: A sequence is an ordered list {a_n}. A series is the sum Σa_n. Convergence of a series is determined by whether the partial sums S_n approach a finite limit L.
Tests include: Ratio Test (|a_{n+1}/a_n|→L), Root Test, Integral Test, Comparison Test, Alternating Series Test. Each applies under different conditions.
The Taylor series of f centred at a is Σ[f^(n)(a)/n!](x-a)^n. For a=0 this is a Maclaurin series. Represents f(x) as an infinite polynomial near x=a.
For f(x,y) the partial derivative ∂f/∂x treats y as constant. Measures how f changes as only x varies. The gradient ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y) points in the direction of steepest ascent.
Double integrals ∬f(x,y)dA integrate over a 2D region. Triple integrals ∭f(x,y,z)dV over a 3D region. Iterated integrals are evaluated one variable at a time.
Extends calculus to vector-valued functions and fields. Key operations: gradient (∇f) divergence (∇·F) curl (∇×F) and line/surface integrals.
